categories_used: Personal care; grocery; dairy; packaged foods
categories_avoided: Electronics; jewellery; clothes; medical products; kitchen appliances
key_barriers: No visible return option in-app; needs to physically demonstrate/test electronics before buying; values personal shopkeeper relationship for trust; if one product experience is bad she never re-tries that category; delivery charge triples the cost of small/low-value orders; no delivery-partner instructions option (e.g. 'knock/ring bell') like Swiggy/Zomato has
trust_factors: Good reviews on the specific product she is considering (not generic suggestions); smooth exchange + guaranteed refund on specific items; low or free delivery on small orders; personal offline relationship
notable_quotes_or_incidents: 'Cost triples for small volume/low price items due to delivery charge'. Never noticed any homepage banner/poster. Would buy anything in top emergency (even electronics) but prefers offline if she has time. Purchase order: reviews first, then price.

categories_used: Packaged snacks; dry fruits; occasional emergency (doormat, bedsheets, charging cable)
key_barriers: Sees quick commerce as a 'last resort'; Blinkit's platform/handling/tax fees are much higher than Myntra/Amazon/Flipkart (which charge just Rs 3-10); prefers to wait for the same product at a lower total cost on a specialist marketplace; trusts specialists over generalists
trust_factors: Specialization + wide range in a category (why he trusts Myntra for clothes, Amazon for electronics); low-value products where fee overhead is tolerable; brand filters
notable_quotes_or_incidents: 'Quick commerce exists because of people's laziness - makes sense only if you're in office with nothing nearby, not at home near a local shop'. Believes quick commerce was normalised by COVID and got over-integrated into daily life. Remembers a 'buy X amount, get products for Rs 1' banner. Never browses homescreen; goes straight to search. Purchase order: price first, then reviews.

order_frequency: Emergency-only; frequency has risen because she is home with a 5-month-old
categories_used: Groceries (packaged foods only now, no fresh)
categories_avoided: Fresh produce (after tomato incident); electronics (Amazon); clothes (Myntra/Flipkart); avoids Blinkit generally due to negative peer stories
key_barriers: Prices ~2x local market on many items (raw peanuts Rs120/kg market vs Rs120/half-kg Blinkit; coconut water Rs70 market vs Rs95 Blinkit); poor customer care with no refunds; unhygienic store perception; refund flow requires camera-only photo capture (no gallery upload) which is unfriendly to less-tech-savvy users; a 'human error tax' - if you forget one item you pay the full delivery charge again for a single item; app showed 'no delivery for a whole week' during Holi when she genuinely needed emergency delivery; class perception: 'Blinkit is for people who don't have to worry about budget'
trust_factors: Friend recommendation combined with price under Rs500; prices within 2-4% of local market
notable_quotes_or_incidents: Tested a viral claim by ordering a tomato in June 2025; by December 2025 it had not rotted (just hardened). This permanently stopped her ordering any fresh items. Neighbour's story: ordered a fan for guests, an important component was missing, embarrassment in front of guests, customer support unresponsive - Astha's takeaway: 'if the order's purpose isn't fulfilled, what's the point of ordering on Blinkit?' Believes categories like electronics and clothing should NOT be forced into 10-min delivery - they need time for quality assurance. Purchase order: reviews first, then brand, then price.

trust_factors: Friend or family recommendation for ANY category (no budget cap); festival-exclusive product launches drive her to browse and try new items
notable_quotes_or_incidents: The most engaged Blinkit user in the sample (3-4 orders/week) yet has already CHURNED for fresh items to a competitor - a warning signal about within-category churn even for power users.
